title: Yusuf and Ya'qub
question: What does patience look like when your own brothers betray you?
intro: Most prophets' stories are spread across many surahs. The story of Yusuf (Joseph) is told almost entirely in one, in order, from a boy's dream to its fulfilment. The Quran calls it "the best of stories" (12:3).

It is a story of envy, betrayal and temptation, but also of a father's patience and a son's integrity. Yusuf falls from his father's love to the bottom of a well, a slave market and a prison, then rises to guard the storehouses of Egypt. At the end he forgives the brothers who wronged him. Watch for the words his father Ya'qub (Jacob) says twice: "patience is most fitting".

passages.context: Yusuf is a boy. His father Ya'qub is the grandson of Ibrahim.
passages.point: Eleven stars, the sun and the moon bow to him. His father senses what it means and warns him to keep it from his brothers. 12:100 shows its fulfilment.
passages.label: stated

passages.context: The brothers had thrown Yusuf into a well (12:15) and came home weeping at night.
passages.point: Ya'qub sees through the false blood but does not rage. He answers with ṣabr jamīl, fitting or beautiful patience, and turns to Allah for help.
passages.label: stated

passages.context: A slave in the house of al-'Aziz, an Egyptian official; his wife is unnamed.
passages.point: He refuses, seeking Allah's refuge, loyal to the master who housed him. Allah turns evil away from him.
passages.label: differ
passages.note: On "he would have inclined to her": many scholars say he never inclined, having seen the proof; others say a passing impulse he did not act on.

passages.context: Years later, famine brings the brothers to Egypt, and they learn the minister before them is Yusuf (12:89-90).
passages.point: With every power to punish, Yusuf forgives at once: "No blame will there be upon you today." He even prays for their forgiveness.
passages.label: stated

visual.title: Yusuf's fall and rise
visual.caption: From a father's favourite to a well, a slave market and a prison, then to the storehouses of Egypt and a family reunited. "Indeed, my Lord is Subtle in what He wills" (12:100).

items.label: The dream
items.text: Eleven stars, the sun and moon bow to him.

items.label: Into the well
items.text: Envious brothers cast him in; Allah reassures him.

items.label: A home in Egypt
items.text: Raised in the house of al-'Aziz.

items.label: Temptation refused
items.text: He seeks Allah's refuge and keeps his integrity.

items.label: Prison
items.text: "Prison is more to my liking." Years pass.

items.label: Dreams explained
items.text: The king's dream: seven fat cows, seven lean.

items.label: Over the stores
items.text: Trusted with Egypt's storehouses through the famine.

items.label: Brothers arrive
items.text: He knows them; they do not know him.

items.label: The dream fulfilled
items.text: His parents raised to the throne; the family bows.

word.nuance: Ṣabr is holding firm: the self kept from panic, the tongue from complaint against Allah. Jamīl, beautiful, adds grace. Ya'qub says it twice, after losing Yusuf (12:18) and then a second son (12:83). The Quran later asks the Prophet ﷺ for the same: "So be patient with gracious patience" (70:5).

mixup.myth: Patience means hiding your grief and never crying.
mixup.truth: Ya'qub wept until "his eyes became white from grief" (12:84), yet the Quran praises his patience. He said, "I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allah" (12:86), and told his sons not to despair (12:87). Patience is not the absence of tears; it is refusing despair and bringing the pain to Allah.

remember: The Quran calls Yusuf's story "the best of stories", told almost entirely in one surah (12:3).
Ya'qub's beautiful patience: grief taken to Allah, never despair of His relief (12:18, 12:86-87).
At the height of his power, Yusuf forgave: "No blame will there be upon you today" (12:92).

quiz.q: What did the brothers bring back to their father as proof?
quiz.why: 12:18: "And they brought upon his shirt false blood." Ya'qub saw through it at once.

quiz.q: Faced with the women's pressure, what did Yusuf say he preferred?
quiz.why: 12:33: "My Lord, prison is more to my liking than that to which they invite me."

quiz.q: What did Yusuf say when his brothers admitted their wrong?
options: "No blame will there be upon you today."
quiz.why: 12:92. He forgave them on the spot and asked Allah to forgive them, "the most merciful of the merciful".

reflect: Ya'qub took his grief to Allah rather than to people. What weight could you hand to Allah in a quiet prayer today?
